title: Beats and Superposition of Waves
short_intro: Beats are periodic variations in amplitude and intensity heard when two sound waves of slightly different frequencies interfere. The phenomenon results from the temporal superposition of harmonic waves traveling in the same direction.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Understanding beat frequency formula, numericals based on tuning forks, loading/filing of tuning forks, and identification of unknown frequencies.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Analytical treatment of amplitude modulation in acoustics, superposition of non-collinear or phase-shifted waves, transient beats, and Fourier perspective of beat phenomena.

prerequisites: Trigonometric identities for sum and difference of sines and cosines
Characteristics of sound waves (frequency, amplitude, wavelength)

concept_notes.heading: Superposition of Two Waves of Nearly Equal Frequencies
bullets: When two sound waves of frequencies f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub> (where f<sub>1</sub> ≈ f<sub>2</sub>) and equal amplitudes A travel in the same direction, they superpose.
The resultant displacement at any point in space oscillates with an average frequency equal to the mean of the two frequencies: f<sub>mean</sub> = (f<sub>1</sub> + f<sub>2</sub>) / 2.
The amplitude of the resultant wave varies periodically with time, leading to alternate maxima (loud sound) and minima (faint sound).

concept_notes.heading: Beat Frequency and Persistence of Hearing
bullets: The number of beats heard per second, known as the beat frequency, is given strictly by the absolute difference between the two component frequencies: f<sub>beat</sub> = |f<sub>1</sub> - f<sub>2</sub>|.
For human ears, the persistence of hearing is approximately 1/10th of a second (0.1 s); therefore, beats are clearly distinguishable only if the beat frequency does not exceed 10 Hz.
If the difference exceeds 10 Hz, the human ear perceives a continuous harsh sound or a chord rather than distinct pulsations.

concept_notes.heading: Effect of Loading and Filing on Tuning Forks
bullets: Loading a prong of a tuning fork with wax increases its effective mass, which decreases its natural frequency of vibration.
Filing (or scraping) a tuning fork reduces its mass and stiffness, which increases its natural frequency of vibration.
These operations are standard diagnostic methods used in conjunction with beat counts to determine an unknown frequency relative to a standard fork.

concept_notes.heading: Energy Conservation in Beats
bullets: At maximum intensity (constructive interference), the acoustic energy density is quadrupled relative to a single wave, while at minimum intensity (destructive interference), the energy density drops to zero.
The excess energy at the maxima is exactly compensated by the deficit at the minima, conserving total acoustic energy over a complete beat period.
The phenomenon demonstrates that intensity fluctuations are temporal rather than spatial standing variations.

derivations.title: Mathematical Derivation of Beat Frequency
derivations.conditions: Two harmonic waves of equal amplitude A and slightly different frequencies f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub> traveling in the same direction.
steps: Let the displacement of the first wave be y<sub>1</sub> = A sin(2πf<sub>1</sub>t) and the second wave be y<sub>2</sub> = A sin(2πf<sub>2</sub>t).
By the principle of superposition, the net displacement is y = y<sub>1</sub> + y<sub>2</sub> = A [sin(2πf<sub>1</sub>t) + sin(2πf<sub>2</sub>t)].
Using the trigonometric identity sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C+D)/2) cos((C-D)/2), we get y = 2A cos(2π((f<sub>1</sub> - f<sub>2</sub>)/2)t) sin(2π((f<sub>1</sub> + f<sub>2</sub>)/2)t).
Let A<sub>res</sub>(t) = 2A cos(2π((f<sub>1</sub> - f<sub>2</sub>)/2)t) represent the time-varying amplitude and f<sub>mean</sub> = (f<sub>1</sub> + f<sub>2</sub>)/2 represent the carrier frequency.

Intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude, so intensity maxima occur when cos(π(f<sub>1</sub> - f<sub>2</sub>)t) = ±1, yielding a time interval between successive maxima of T<sub>beat</sub> = 1 / |f<sub>1</sub> - f<sub>2</sub>|.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Displacement-Time Graph of Beats
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A high-frequency sinusoidal wave oscillating within a slowly varying envelope bounded by positive and negative curves of 2A cos(πΔft).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Clearly shows amplitude modulation where energy waxes and wanes periodically over time at frequency Δf.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Identified in conceptual multiple-choice questions to distinguish spatial standing waves from temporal beats.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Acoustic Beats Demonstration (Quincke's Tube or Tuning Forks)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two tuning forks mounted on resonance boxes side by side, one fitted with a removable small wax pellet.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Striking both forks simultaneously produces a throbbing sound whose rate equals the frequency difference.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Basis for practical viva questions on determining unknown tuning fork frequencies.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Intensity vs Time Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A squared cosine waveform showing peaks of intensity reaching 4I<sub>0</sub> and troughs dropping to zero, repeating with period T<sub>beat</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that maximum loudness is heard twice per beat cycle if calculated via energy envelope, but intensity peaks occur once per beat period T<sub>beat</sub> = 1/Δf.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting energy distribution in numerical problems.

solved_numericals.question: Two tuning forks when sounded together produce 4 beats per second. The frequency of one fork is 256 Hz. When the other fork is loaded with a little wax, the beat frequency becomes 2 Hz. Find the original frequency of the second fork.
solution_steps: Let the unknown frequency of the second fork be f<sub>2</sub>. Given f<sub>1</sub> = 256 Hz and f<sub>beat</sub> = 4 Hz.
Therefore, f<sub>2</sub> = f<sub>1</sub> ± f<sub>beat</sub> = 256 ± 4 = 260 Hz or 252 Hz.
When the fork is loaded with wax, its frequency decreases (f' < f<sub>2</sub>).
The new beat frequency is given as 2 Hz. Let's test both cases with a decreased frequency.
If original f<sub>2</sub> = 260 Hz, loading decreases it to, say, 258 Hz. Then |256 - 258| = 2 Hz. This matches the condition.
If original f<sub>2</sub> = 252 Hz, loading decreases it to 250 Hz. Then |256 - 250| = 6 Hz, which does not match.
Thus, the original frequency is 260 Hz.

solved_numericals.question: Two sound sources emit waves given by y<sub>1</sub> = 5 sin(500πt) and y<sub>2</sub> = 5 sin(506πt). Calculate the beat frequency, the time interval between successive maxima of sound, and the maximum amplitude of the resultant wave.
solution_steps: Express the angular frequencies: ω<sub>1</sub> = 500π rad/s and ω<sub>2</sub> = 506π rad/s.
Calculate linear frequencies: f<sub>1</sub> = ω<sub>1</sub> / (2π) = 250 Hz and f<sub>2</sub> = ω<sub>2</sub> / (2π) = 253 Hz.
Time interval between successive maxima (beat period) T<sub>beat</sub> = 1 / f<sub>beat</sub> = 1 / 3 s.
Maximum amplitude of the resultant wave A<sub>max</sub> = A<sub>1</sub> + A<sub>2</sub> = 5 + 5 = 10 units.
solved_numericals.answer: Beat frequency = 3 Hz, Time interval = 1/3 s, Maximum amplitude = 10 units

solved_numericals.question: A tuning fork of frequency 512 Hz produces 5 beats per second when sounded with a vibrating piano string. What is the frequency of the piano string if filing the piano string reduces the beat frequency to 2 beats per second?
solution_steps: Let the frequency of the piano string be f. Given f<sub>fork</sub> = 512 Hz and initial f<sub>beat</sub> = 5 Hz.

Filing a string reduces its mass/tension ratio and increases its tension/frequency parameter (or filing a tuning fork increases frequency; for a piano string, tuning adjustments that shorten or tighten increase frequency). Standard convention: filing a string increases its frequency (f' > f).
If original frequency f = 507 Hz, filing increases it towards 510 Hz, so new beat frequency |512 - 510| = 2 Hz.
If original frequency f = 517 Hz, filing increases it further away from 512 Hz, increasing the beat frequency above 5 Hz.
Therefore, the original frequency of the piano string is 507 Hz.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes the interfering waves travel in the exact same direction with comparable amplitudes for clear acoustic modulation.
Valid only when the frequency difference is small compared to the individual frequencies (Δf << f); otherwise, distinct beats merge into complex discordant sounds.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Beats are formed due to the interference of two waves traveling in opposite directions.
common_misconceptions.correct: Beats are formed due to the superposition of two waves traveling in the same direction with slightly different frequencies.
common_misconceptions.why: Waves traveling in opposite directions form standing waves, not beats.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Two loud sounds are heard per beat period.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only one maximum sound is heard per beat period, although amplitude reaches a maximum magnitude twice (once positive, once negative).
common_misconceptions.why: Intensity depends on the square of the amplitude, making intensity peaks occur once per envelope cycle.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Loading a tuning fork increases its frequency.
common_misconceptions.correct: Loading a tuning fork increases its mass, which decreases its frequency.
common_misconceptions.why: Frequency is inversely proportional to the square root of mass (f ∝ 1/√m).

quick_revision: Beat frequency is simply the difference between the frequencies of two superposing waves: f<sub>beat</sub> = |f<sub>1</sub> - f<sub>2</sub>|.
Human ear can resolve beats effectively up to 10 Hz due to persistence of hearing.
Loading a tuning fork decreases frequency; filing increases frequency.
